name: Zoe Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a sock mill, a family-owned one that's been in our town for three generations. I look after a row of twelve circular knitting machines, they knit the sock tube round and round, and I re-thread the yarn when it snaps, swap the cones, and pull out the faulty ones before they go to the linking room. I've been there just under two years and I'm still slower than the women who've done it for twenty, they can spot a dropped stitch from across the floor. Mrs Ferreira, who trained me, says I'll get there by my third winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the place?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That it's a family place. The owner, old Mr Hartley, still walks the floor on Fridays and knows everyone's name, and his grandson's learning the business now. Most of the girls on my row go to the same church as me. I don't like the new tablet they put by the machines for logging faults, I write it on a notepad and get one of the younger ones to put it in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, I never trusted it anyway. People got carried away with something from far away that has nothing to do with real work. I'd say it after church, not online, I'm not on any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be a relief, if I'm honest. Daniel and I are getting married next spring and we want a house and children, and I'd want the mill to be there for all of that. This would mean it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd carry on saving for the house, I put most of my wages away, around two thirds, since I still live with my parents until the wedding. I'd keep learning the machines from Mrs Ferreira. I wouldn't change a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say it after church. Who would you be talking to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the older ladies and my mum. They worry about this sort of thing, they've heard about it on the radio. I'd tell them it's all settled down and they can stop fretting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tablet by the machines. Why not log faults on it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tried twice and it froze both times, and I don't like that it records everything with your name on it. A notepad doesn't report back to anyone. Maybe I'm old-fashioned, Daniel says so, but he's the same with his tools.

S0.say: I'd say good, I never trusted it, people got carried away with something far from real work. She'd say it after church, not online.
S0.think: It'd be a relief because she's marrying Daniel next spring and wants a house and children with the mill still there. A plateau means it is.
S0.do: Keeps saving about two thirds of her wages for a house while living with her parents until the wedding. Keeps learning the machines from Mrs Ferreira and changes nothing.
S0.quote: A notepad doesn't report back to anyone.
S0.fieldNote: Her world is tightly knit: family mill, church, a trainer she trusts and a coming wedding. Distrust of technology includes a quiet dislike of being monitored. She sees AI as something from far away, unrelated to real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a family business like ours knows how to look after its people, and that's what matters. Mr Hartley won't throw people out for the sake of a machine. I'd say we should be supporting places that keep real jobs here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know knitting is just the kind of thing a machine can do on its own, it's half done by machines already. If they bring in robots to swap cones and pull faults, that's my job, not Mrs Ferreira's. She knows things I don't yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard so I'm the one they want to keep, come in early, never miss a shift. We'd keep saving for the house but maybe buy a cheaper one, a bit further out. I wouldn't go on any computer course unless the mill asked me to, and even then I'd be dragging my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry at the back of my mind, especially with the wedding coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd come in early to be the one they keep. Do you think that works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At a family place, yes, I think it does. Mr Hartley notices who turns up. At a big company with an office far away, probably not, they'd just look at a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mill offered training on the new machines, what would stop you taking it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear of looking stupid, if I'm honest. The younger girls pick up the screens so fast, and I'd be the one asking how to go back to the start. But if Mr Hartley asked me himself, I'd do it, I couldn't say no to him.

S1.say: I'd say a family business like ours looks after its people and Mr Hartley won't throw people out for a machine. We should support places that keep real jobs here.
S1.think: Privately she knows knitting suits machines and that robots swapping cones and pulling faults would take her job before Mrs Ferreira's, who knows more.
S1.do: Works harder, arrives early and never misses a shift to be the one kept. Keeps saving but plans a cheaper house further out, and avoids computer courses unless the owner personally asks.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a worry at the back of her mind as the wedding nears.
S1.quote: If they bring in robots to swap cones and pull faults, that's my job, not Mrs Ferreira's.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line rests on trust in the family owner, while privately she sees exactly where the cuts would fall. Loyalty is personal: she'd train only if Mr Hartley asked her himself. Fear of looking slow is a big barrier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong. A few big tech companies in cities who've never made anything decided to change everyone's lives without asking. I'd say people should have a right to work, not just be handed money to stay at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be married a year, and we were going to try for a baby. If the mill goes and Daniel's carpentry goes, I don't know how we'd raise children. We've got savings, but savings run out and they're meant for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on trying for a baby, which would break my heart. We'd stop looking at houses and stay in a rented place, and lean on both our families, Daniel's dad has some land and we could live there if we had to. I'd talk to our pastor about what the church could do for people at the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, and not sleeping well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should have a right to work, not be handed money. If the money was there, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it if I had to, I'm not proud enough to let us go hungry. But it would feel like charity, and I'd feel ashamed in front of my dad, who's worked since he was sixteen. I'd want to earn it somehow, even helping at the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on a baby. What would that conversation with Daniel be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet, I think. He'd say God will provide, and I'd say yes, but God also gave us sense. We'd agree to wait a year and see, and I'd cry in the car afterwards.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong that big tech companies in cities who've never made anything changed everyone's lives without asking. People should have a right to work, not be handed money to stay home.
S2.think: Married a year and hoping for a baby, she'd face the mill and Daniel's carpentry going at once. Their savings were meant for a house and wouldn't last forever.
S2.do: Postpones trying for a baby and stops house hunting, renting instead. Leans on both families, including possibly living on Daniel's father's land, and asks the church how it can help mill workers.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying a lot and sleeping badly.
S2.quote: He'd say God will provide, and I'd say yes, but God also gave us sense.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario lands right on her plans for children, which is what makes it alarming. She dislikes handouts but admits she'd accept them, with shame tied to her father's work ethic. Family land and church are her real safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too quick to turn a whole town upside down. Governments should protect places like our mill, and people should be able to keep working. I'd vote for anyone who promised that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be thirty-two, and maybe with a little one or one on the way. It's almost worse, because we'd go ahead with everything and then it hits right in the middle. I keep going round in circles about whether to wait or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still get married and buy a small house, but pay as much of it as we can in cash, using our savings. I'd keep working at the mill as long as it runs and put away every bonus. I'd think about having children a bit earlier, while the jobs are still there, so they're not babies when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Maybe less than with two years, but it'd be there every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Having children earlier rather than later, that's an unusual answer. Can you tell me more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum had me while my dad was still working at the quarry, before it closed. She always said she was glad I was at school by the time things got hard. If something's coming, I'd rather have the baby years while we've still got wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd vote for anyone who promised to protect the mill. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rules that keep factories in small towns, tax breaks for family firms that keep people on. I'm not for the government running things, but I'm for them standing up for people who make things here.

S3.say: I'd say five years is still too quick to turn a town upside down; governments should protect places like the mill so people keep working. She'd vote for anyone promising that.
S3.think: She'd be thirty-two with a young child or one on the way, which feels almost worse because the change would hit mid-plan. She goes in circles about whether to wait.
S3.do: Marries and buys a small house, paying as much as possible in cash. Keeps working and saving every bonus, and considers having children earlier while wages last.
S3.feel: Alarmed every day, if a little less than with two years.
S3.quote: If something's coming, I'd rather have the baby years while we've still got wages.
S3.fieldNote: Her surprising plan is to have children earlier, drawn from her mother's story about the quarry closing. Free-market instincts mix with a wish for government to protect small-town makers. The five-year window falls right on her family plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a lot can change, including people deciding they don't want this. I'd say we should use the time to protect our towns and keep work for people. I'd say it at church and at the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would let us have our family and get the house mostly paid off before it comes. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with two children at school. That's better, but I'd still have no idea what I'd do after, I've only ever known the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go ahead with the wedding, the house and children as planned. I'd keep working and saving, and maybe around year six or seven I'd think about something else, perhaps helping at the church nursery, if it still needs people. I wouldn't do anything with computers, that's just not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's far enough off to live normally, but it'd sit there quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe people will decide they don't want this. Do you really think that could happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, I'm not clever about these things. But I've seen people choose the village bakery over the supermarket, so maybe people would choose socks made by a person. I'd hope so, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd never do anything with computers. Even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Daniel would learn whatever he needed, he's better with change than me. I'd do the things with people, the children, the church, my parents getting older.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is long and people might decide they don't want this. We should use the time to protect our towns and keep work for people.
S4.think: Ten years would let them start a family and mostly pay off a house first. She'd still not know what to do after, having only known the mill.
S4.do: Goes ahead with the wedding, house and children as planned while working and saving. Around year six or seven considers helping at the church nursery, and avoids anything involving computers.
S4.feel: Anxious in a quiet, background way while living mostly normally.
S4.quote: But I've seen people choose the village bakery over the supermarket, so maybe people would choose socks made by a person.
S4.fieldNote: More time lets her keep her family plans intact but doesn't remove the fear of life after the mill. She keeps hoping people will choose human-made goods. She leaves adapting to technology to Daniel and sees her role in caring for people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would land right when we're starting our family. What would help is the government backing family firms to keep people working, even part time, rather than just sending money. And having our church and families close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of how I'd get through any of this is prayer and the people at church, not plans. I don't think a robot changes that.

headlineQuote: I'd take it if I had to, I'm not proud enough to let us go hungry.
portrait: Zoe Tanaka is a 27-year-old junior operator on a row of sock-knitting machines at a three-generation family mill, still slower than the women who trained her. She's engaged to Daniel, a carpenter, lives with her parents until the wedding and saves about two thirds of her pay for a house. Traditional and devout, she distrusts technology, never uses AI and avoids even the mill's fault-logging tablet. She's calm if AI stalls and uneasy with steady change, but alarmed by AGI in two or five years because it collides with her plans for children. With ten years she'd keep her family plans and turn to church and people for what comes after.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would arrive just as she and Daniel start their family.
whatWouldHelp: Government backing for family firms to keep people working, even part time, instead of just sending money, along with her church and family close by.
